description: Make some fun sounds from images
summary:
Earth Jukebox — hear 46 years of NASA Earth science as music

NASA's Earth Information Center produces extraordinary visualisations of our changing planet, but presenting Earth science only as images excludes blind and low‑vision audiences. Earth Jukebox turns those visual frames into sound in real time. We pull NASA GIBS MERRA‑2 monthly rasters, decode every pixel back into a physical value using NASA's own published colour bars, and aggregate them onto a 10° global grid — 560 monthly frames from January 1980 to August 2026 across five variables: air temperature, precipitation, wind speed, aerosol optical depth and root‑zone soil moisture. Two places then sound simultaneously, one in each ear, as a browser‑synthesised ensemble in which each variable is played by the sound of the physical process it measures: rain falls as droplets, wind breathes as filtered noise, dust thickens a chord‑tuned sub‑bass, soil moisture becomes a fingerpicked guitar arpeggio, and temperature sets the register of a plucked nylon‑guitar melody built from Karplus‑Strong strings. A listener can scrub through 46 years of climate history and hear the Arctic warm, the monsoon arrive and the Sahara fall silent — no installation, no audio files, no server.
details:
What it does and how it works. Earth Jukebox is a single web app that sonifies NASA Earth science data in real time. The pipeline has three stages:

  1. Ingest (offline, Python). tools/ingest.py requests NASA GIBS WMS GetMap rasters for five MERRA‑2 monthly layers for every month from 1980‑01 to 2026‑08 (560 frames). Each pixel is converted back to a physical number by inverting NASA's own published colour bar for that layer (tools/make_ramps.py), then aggregated onto a 36×18 grid at 10° resolution. The result is a 2.4 MB dataset (data/dataset.json → packed to app/data/dataset.js).
    • Temperature → the register of a plucked guitar melody (10 scale steps ≈ 1.5 octaves) plus note length and brightness.
    • Precipitation → droplet hits whose rate (0.35→10/s), pitch and level follow rainfall; a dry month is genuinely silent.
    • Wind speed → a band of breathing noise; level, centre frequency (300→1200 Hz) and LFO rate all follow speed, and wind also triggers a high "sparkle" layer.
    • Aerosol optical depth → a warm sub‑bass tuned to the chord root, so dust thickens the harmony from below.
    • Soil moisture → the density of a fingerpicked guitar arpeggio inside the chord.
    • A shared four‑chord progression keeps both ears consonant: side A is Dorian on A2, side B is Lydian on E3, a fifth apart. Nothing is sustained — every voice is struck and decays, so a 46‑year scan never turns into a drone.

Benefits. For blind and low‑vision users it converts a visualisation they cannot access into a continuously listenable stream that carries the actual numbers, with a screen‑reader live region narrating date, both places, all five values and the musical register. For sighted users it makes 46 years of climate change perceptible in about 100 seconds — the Arctic's warming is audible as a rising register, and the Arctic/global contrast is audible as a difference between the two ears. Because both sides obey identical mapping rules, any difference you hear is a real difference in the data.

Intended impact. A demonstration that accessibility is not a retrofit: a sonification can be a genuine instrument, not a beeping chart. The technique generalises to any NASA variable that has a published colour bar — the app is a template for turning EIC imagery into an accessible, broadcastable, museum‑loopable channel.

Tools, languages, software. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks, no bundler, no CDN, no third‑party libraries). Web Audio API (OscillatorNode, AudioBufferSourceNode, BiquadFilterNode, StereoPannerNode, ConvolverNode, DynamicsCompressorNode) and Canvas 2D. Ingest and QA in Python 3 with numpy, pillow and playwright (headless Chromium). No hardware beyond the listener's browser.

How it is creative. The creative decision was to make each variable sound like itself rather than like a parameter. Dust does not get a tune — it thickens the bass. Heat does not raise a beep — it moves the melody into a higher register inside a shared harmony. Two places are heard as two characters in one key rather than two data streams, so the piece can be listened to for hours. It also documents its own failures: the design notes record six earlier versions (sawtooth drone, sustained pad, fixed motif, organ, physical models, guitar) and why each was rejected — the tune that was "ours rather than the planet's" was the hardest one to give up.

Factors considered. Data fidelity vs. musicality (quantising a continuous curve onto a scale loses precision — documented honestly); accessibility as a first‑class path (keyboard‑only operation, ARIA slider, narrated live region, reduced‑motion and contrast support); performance (a 46‑year scan on a laptop, cached strings, compressor + limiter so nothing clips); honesty of representation (the app is explicit that it is reanalysis data on a 10° display grid, ~0.2 K colour‑bar quantisation, monthly resolution); and licensing/attribution (NASA data credited, MIT code, no copyrighted assets).
